h1: Setting up a fermentation corner in a rented flat
title: A Fermentation Corner in a Rented Flat | Craft Beer School
desc: Where to put a fermenter in a rented flat, how to keep it cool in Indian heat and how to avoid spills, smells and trouble with the landlord.
teaser: Your fermenter needs a cool, dark, quiet spot that survives a spill. In a rented flat that takes a little planning.
standfirst: Most homebrewers in Indian cities rent. That rules out drilling, rewiring or taking over the balcony. Here is how we set up a fermentation corner that keeps the beer at the right temperature and leaves the deposit intact.
sections: Temperature decides where the corner goes

Yeast cares about one thing more than any other in your flat: temperature. Most ale yeasts work best between about 18 and 20 °C. Indian rooms in summer sit at 28 to 35 °C. On top of that, active fermentation generates its own heat. A vigorous 20 litre ferment can run several degrees above the room around it.

So the best spot is the coolest one, not the most convenient one. Walk the flat with a cheap digital thermometer for a few days. Check the floor, not shoulder height, because cool air sinks. An inner wall away from the afternoon sun almost always wins. A bathroom with a tiled floor is often the coolest room in the flat.

Avoid the kitchen. Cooking adds heat several times a day and the air carries oil and flour dust that you do not want near an open fermenter on transfer day. Avoid the top of the fridge too. The coils at the back push out warm air, so that shelf is often the warmest spot in the room.
Keep it dark and keep it still

Light is the second enemy. Ultraviolet and blue light react with hop compounds in finished beer to produce a skunky aroma. A glass carboy near a window is the worst case. Cover clear fermenters with a towel or a cardboard box. Plastic buckets are opaque, which helps.

Choose a spot where nobody will bump the fermenter. Moving it after day three stirs up settling yeast and can splash oxygen into the beer. Corners behind doors, under a bed or inside a wardrobe all work if the temperature is right.

Think about access too. You will need to read a strip thermometer twice a day and lift the fermenter out after two weeks. A full 20 litre fermenter weighs over 20 kg. Pick a spot you can reach without crouching under furniture while holding it.

Sooner or later a fermentation will climb out of its airlock. Krausen, the foam on top of fermenting beer, is sticky and stains grout. Stand the fermenter in a plastic tray or a shallow tub. In the first three days of an active ferment, swap the airlock for a blow-off tube running into a jar of sanitiser.

The tub doubles as cooling. Fill it with water and you have the start of a swamp cooler, which can hold a fermenter several degrees below room temperature. Our guide to using a swamp cooler explains the method.
Smell and carbon dioxide in a small space

Fermentation smells of bread, fruit and sometimes sulphur for the first few days. In a two-room flat that is noticeable. A blow-off jar of sanitiser cuts most of it. A bathroom with an exhaust fan solves the rest.

A 20 litre batch releases carbon dioxide over several days. In a normal ventilated room that is not a hazard. Do not ferment inside a closed cupboard you then put your head into. Leave the door open for a minute before reaching in.

Everything in the corner should come out the day you move. Use plug-in temperature controllers rather than anything hard-wired. Use a second-hand fridge or chest freezer only if the flat has a spare socket that can take it without an extension board daisy chain. Compressor appliances draw a surge on start-up, so plug them straight into a wall socket rather than a cheap multi-plug.

If you graduate to a fermentation fridge, our guide to fermentation temperature control at home covers the options. Rules on home production of alcohol vary by state in India, so check what applies where you live.
Measure the beer, not the room

A thermometer on the wall tells you about the air. The yeast lives in the wort. Stick a liquid crystal strip thermometer on the side of the fermenter, below the liquid line. It reads close to the beer itself and costs very little.

Check it morning and evening for the first four days, when fermentation is most active and runs warmest. If the strip reads above 22 °C during that window for a clean ale, add frozen bottles to the water tub. Knowing which yeast tolerates heat and which throws harsh flavours is the kind of judgement that turns a corner into a reliable process.
Start with a week of readings

Before your next brew, place a thermometer in three candidate spots and note the lowest and highest reading each day for a week. Pick the spot with the smallest swing and the lowest peak. Put a tray there, add a tub of water and stand an empty fermenter in it so you know it fits. Then brew.
faqs: Where is the coolest place to ferment beer in a flat?
Usually the floor of an inner room or a tiled bathroom away from afternoon sun. Measure for a few days before deciding.
Is the carbon dioxide from fermentation dangerous at home?
In a normally ventilated room, a homebrew batch is not a hazard. Avoid fermenting in a sealed cupboard and opening it with your face in the doorway.
Can I ferment on a balcony?
Only if it is fully shaded all day. Direct sun heats a fermenter fast and light damages hop aroma, so most balconies are worse than an inner room.
